name: Parallel workflow
purpose: One bounded graph run started from ordinary chat that may split the work: a slicing step reads the mandate and divides it into two or three slices with their own owned paths, or keeps it as one slice when it does not split well; the implementing step then runs one branch per slice at the same time, each in its own session and its own worktree from one recorded base; an integrating step merges the branches into the working copy, resolves conflicts and checks the combination, and may send the work back to the branches with concrete findings; an independent review then finds the assignment met, sends it back, or finds that it cannot be met. The engine never merges. Branches can send each other messages while they run, delivered only when the recipient next checks; contract changes they propose are open proposals the integrating step resolves. Run it on a clean working copy: with uncommitted changes to tracked files every branch's base holds them, git merge refuses, and the integrating step stops BLOCKED rather than move the person's work aside. The concurrency caps (Claude 3, Copilot 3, Cursor 1) come from reading the adapters' code and have not been observed with a live provider.
notes: DSP-209 S10c. The first bundled loop that runs work in parallel, and the drawing that records the decisions behind it: the vision's structured parallel execution, integration and ownership (ADAPTIVE_EXECUTION_AND_SHARED_CONTEXT.md); the reconciliation in CONTROLLED_PARALLELISM_AND_DIALOGUE_BASED_GRAPH_DESIGN.md §10; and DSP-209's mission decisions 5 (fan-out within one visit, the walk stays one node at a time), 6 (one base: HEAD, or a git stash create commit), 7 (the integrator is a role and it merges), 22 (caps Claude 3, Copilot 3, Cursor 1, read from code and not observed), 23 (messages between branches only at check_messages, not built yet), 24 (at most six slices; temporary branches kept for Niclas), 25-26 (the split and the ownership rule) and 27 (branches run on a contained path with no snapshot of their own). Since DSP-209 S11 the branches have a mailbox (decisions 8, 9, 23): send_message, check_messages and acknowledge_message, delivery only at a check, no wait, no restart for a message, and the person's instructions during the fan-out reach every branch the same way. With uncommitted changes to tracked files the merge stops BLOCKED (S10c finding). Splitting is optional: one slice is a fan-out of one branch, which is how the slicer serialises or combines work that does not split well. Branch names carry the node and its visit (dspatch/run/<runId>/<node>/v<visit>/<slice>), so a rework back to the implementing step makes new branches beside the first visit's. Not the chat loop, not the development loop and not the mission loop; none of them is changed by this one.

limits.note: All guesses, recorded as guesses (DSP-209 S10c). The slicer, three branches, the integrator and review are six calls; one rework from the integrator back to the branches is four more, and one review rework back to the integrator is two more, so 14 calls leaves room for one of each. The implementing step's 60 minutes bound its whole visit, every branch included; under Cursor's cap of one, its branches run one after another inside that. None of it has been measured.

failureKinds.label: specification error
failureKinds.meaning: The task's premise is wrong and the work cannot be done as asked. The run stops rather than inventing a different task.

failureKinds.label: blocked
failureKinds.meaning: A concrete obstacle prevents the work: missing access, or a decision this run cannot make.

failureKinds.label: a branch failed
failureKinds.meaning: A branch faulted, timed out or produced nothing, or the slice block could not be run. Every branch's work is kept on its temporary branch or in its kept worktree.

failureKinds.label: correction rounds spent
failureKinds.meaning: DSpatch's bound on correction rounds was spent while the work was still being sent back. DSpatch routes this when the bound is reached; no step declares it.

nodes.label: Split the work
nodes.purpose:
Read the Mandate and the project, and decide whether the work splits into two or three parts that can be done at the same time without writing the same files. Write one dspatch-slices block: two or three slices, or a single slice when it does not split well. Each slice names its result, the paths it owns, its allowed actions, the contracts it works against and its smallest check. Do not change any file.

Write the plan as exactly one fenced block whose info string is `dspatch-slices`, in the form this message gives; DSpatch reads exactly one.

If the premise of the mandate is wrong, begin your reply with the word SPEC_ERROR and then one sentence saying what is wrong. If something concrete prevents the work, begin your reply with the word BLOCKED and then one sentence saying what is in the way.

produces.note: Exactly one dspatch-slices block, and a short account of why the work was split this way or kept whole.

nodes.notes: The slicer is a role and nothing more (the parallelism document's §7): nothing in the engine treats this node specially. Its result is required, because the implementing step's branches are made from the block in it.

nodes.label: Do the slices
nodes.purpose:
Do your slice of the Mandate, in your own worktree, inside the paths your slice owns, and run your slice's check. On a later visit you are given the integrating step's findings: act on the ones that concern your slice.

You are one of several agents doing the same assignment in parallel, each with its own slice. Your message ends with **your slice**: its result, the paths you own, your allowed actions, the contracts you work against and your check. Do that slice, and only that slice.

Work in the folder you were given: your own worktree, made from the same base as every other branch. Read freely there.

Change **only the paths your slice owns**. Another branch owns the rest, and if two branches change the same file the integrating step has to undo one of them. When your slice cannot be done without changing a path you do not own, do not change it: say which path and why in your reply, so the integrating step can decide.

Work against the contracts your slice names. If one turns out to be inadequate, do not quietly change the shared agreement; say what is wrong and what you assumed instead.

Run **your slice's own check**, as the slice names it, and fix what it shows. Run the last check after your last change. Do not run the whole project's suite: the integrating step checks the combination.

On a later visit you are given the integrating step's findings. Act on the ones that concern your slice.

**Messages between the branches.** You have three tools for the other branches running beside you: `check_messages`, `send_message` and `acknowledge_message`.

- Call `check_messages` at natural boundaries: **before you start**, **after a significant change**, and **before you finish**. Messages are delivered only when you check; nothing interrupts your work.
- Send a `finding` when something you found affects another slice's owned paths or a contract the slices share — to that slice by its id, or to `all`. Send a `question` when another slice's answer would change what you do, and carry on without the answer. Send a `contract-change` when a shared contract has to change: it is a proposal for the integrating step to resolve, not an agreement, so do not build on it as if it were decided. Send to `integrator` what only the integrating step can resolve.
- `acknowledge_message` a message once you have acted on it.
- A message from `the person` is the person's instruction to the run: follow it as part of your assignment, within your slice.
- **Never wait for a reply.** There is no way to wait, and a branch that has ended is not restarted for a message. Keep messages short and to the point; routine progress is not a message.

Do not commit, push, switch branches or create branches. When your turn ends, DSpatch commits what you left in your worktree to your temporary branch, and the integrating step merges the branches. Do not install dependencies, change global configuration or touch anything outside your worktree.

Reply in prose: what is now true of your slice, the files you changed and why, what you ran and what it showed for the code as you leave it, and anything you could not do or had to assume — a path you needed and did not own, a contract you found inadequate.

If the premise of your slice is wrong, begin your reply with the word SPEC_ERROR and then one sentence saying what is wrong. If something concrete prevents the work, begin your reply with the word BLOCKED and then one sentence saying what is in the way.

produces.note: Written by DSpatch: per slice, how it ended, its temporary branch and commit, and its reply, clipped.

nodes.notes: The one fan-out node. Each slice runs as its own branch instance; DSpatch commits what each left to its temporary branch and removes its worktree, or keeps the worktree when the commit is refused. The step's own result lists every branch, its commit and its reply, clipped; the integrator reads the commits.

nodes.label: Combine the branches
nodes.purpose:
Merge each slice's temporary branch into the working copy in the order the slices were listed, resolve conflicts, check that the branches respect the contracts the slices named, and run the checks the combination needs. Name what you merged, from which branch and commit, and what conflicted and how you resolved it. If a branch has to be redone, declare rework with concrete findings for the slices concerned. Never delete a temporary branch.

Each slice's temporary branch is named `dspatch/run/<run>/<node>/v<visit>/<slice>`, and a rework visit's branches carry the next visit number.

`integrated` when every branch is merged and the combination checks out as far as you can tell; `rework` with findings for the branches when one has to be redone; `not-integrated` when the branches cannot be combined into what the mandate asks. The independent review that follows is not your check; do not treat your own `integrated` as it.

If the premise of the mandate is wrong, begin your reply with the word SPEC_ERROR and then one sentence saying what is wrong. If something concrete prevents the work, begin your reply with the word BLOCKED and then one sentence saying what is in the way.

produces.note: Exactly what was merged, from which branch and commit, what conflicted and how it was resolved, and what was checked. On rework, the findings for each slice concerned.

nodes.notes: Decision 7: the integrator merges; the engine does not. It is handed the implementing step's result, which names every branch and commit; it reads the commits, not the clipped replies.

nodes.label: Check the combined work
nodes.purpose:
Establish independently whether the assignment was met by the combined work in the working copy. Discover how this project is checked and run those checks yourself where your tools can run commands. Judge from real results, not from the integrating step's account. If the combination can be fixed, say exactly what is wrong and declare rework; if it is met, declare met; if it cannot be met, declare not-met.

Reply in prose, to the person who reads this run. They may not have read the role and should not have to.

DSpatch lets a `met` stand only if a command recorded in this run completed on the code exactly as you leave it, or if the run changed no file. Run your checks on the code as it is, and do not change files.

`met` means the assignment was met. `rework` means it was not met yet and the work step can fix it: list each finding concretely — the command you ran, what it showed, and what has to change — because your reply is the only thing the work step is given about what is wrong. `not-met` means it cannot be met as asked, or what is wrong is not something another round of work would fix; say why. `could-not-check` means you could not establish it — no identifiable check, a command you could not run, or a result you could not read. Use `could-not-check` rather than guessing. It is a real answer and not a failure of the run.

Do not declare `limit-reached`. DSpatch routes that itself when the correction rounds are spent.

If the premise of the check is wrong, begin your reply with the word SPEC_ERROR and then one sentence saying what is wrong. If something concrete prevents the check — access you do not have, a decision that is not yours — begin your reply with the word BLOCKED and then one sentence saying what is in the way. Those two words are read only as the opening of your reply, so use either of them freely in ordinary prose anywhere else.

produces.note: Your verdict and findings. On rework they are the only thing the integrating step is given about what is wrong.

nodes.notes: The same independent check as the chat loop's, on the integrated result: its own session, so it did not watch the work happen.

nodes.label: Assignment met
nodes.purpose: The independent review declared that the combined work met the assignment. That is its named verdict. The temporary branches are kept for you to keep or delete.

nodes.label: Assignment not met
nodes.purpose: The review or the integrating step declared that the assignment cannot be met, or the correction rounds were spent. What was merged is in the working copy; the temporary branches are kept.

nodes.label: Could not establish
nodes.purpose: The run could not establish whether the assignment was met: the review could not decide, or it was blocked or wrongly specified. This is not a pass and not a failure of the project.

nodes.label: A branch failed
nodes.purpose: A branch faulted, timed out or produced nothing, or the slice block could not be run, so the work was not combined. Each branch's work is kept on its temporary branch, or in its worktree when it could not be committed; the run's record lists them.

nodes.label: Stopped without doing the work
nodes.purpose: A step reported that the premise was wrong or that it was blocked, so the work was not done or not finished. Its own sentence is in the conversation.

edges.label: back to the branches with findings
edges.notes: The second visit to the fan-out: new branches beside the first visit's, each given the integrating step's findings. Counted against maxReworkRounds.

edges.label: not met: back to the integrator with findings
edges.notes: The review's findings go to the integrating step, which may fix the combination itself or send the branches back.
